title: Brick to marble
saying: marmoream sē relinquere, quam laterīciam accēpisset
author: Suetonius

edition.name: Suetonius, De Vita Caesarum, vol. I (Julius, Augustus), Latin text of the Loeb Classical Library edition (J. C. Rolfe), as presented on LacusCurtius (Bill Thayer), whose Latin pages credit it, in their own wording, to "a Loeb Classical Library editi[on] MCMXIII" (1913), public domain

source_text: Urbem neque pro maiestate imperii ornatam et inundationibus incendiisque obnoxiam excoluit adeo, ut iure sit gloriatus marmoream se relinquere, quam latericiam accepisset.

macrons.note: Macrons are editorial: added by Vocābula, not printed in the edition. Vowel quantities follow the app lexicon (Wheelock / DCC spellings) where the word is in it, and standard dictionary quantities otherwise.
uncertain: maiestāte: the first syllable is written without a macron (maiestās), the convention of the app's textbook for a vowel before consonantal i; some dictionaries print māiestās. The syllable is heavy either way.
laterīciam: long ī, from the material suffix -īcius (as in caementīcius). I could not fetch a dictionary entry for latericius to confirm it; treat it as uncertain.
imperiī: written with -iī; Suetonius's period may well have pronounced and written -ī.

translation: The city was not adorned as the greatness of the empire deserved, and it was exposed to floods and fires; he improved it so much that he could rightly boast that he was leaving in marble the city he had received in brick.
translation_note: The boast is in indirect statement (sē relinquere), so these are not necessarily Augustus's exact words: Suetonius does not quote him directly.

essay.t: Suetonius sets the scene in two clauses: Rome was not adorned as an imperial capital should be, and it was exposed to floods and fires.
Augustus, he says, improved it so much that he could rightly boast of leaving a city of marble where he had found one of brick.
The boast is reported in indirect speech, so the passage does not claim to give Augustus's exact words.
Cassius Dio does give them directly, in a different form: during his last illness Augustus told his associates, "I found Rome of clay; I leave it to you of marble."
Dio then adds that Augustus did not mean the look of the buildings but the strength of the empire.
So the two historians agree on a saying but disagree on its wording, its occasion and even its meaning, and we cannot decide between them from these texts alone.
The buildings themselves are well attested.
Suetonius goes on to list them, beginning with the Forum with the temple of Mars Ultor, the temple of Apollo on the Palatine and the temple of Jupiter the Thunderer on the Capitol.

In his own account of his achievements, Augustus says he rebuilt eighty-two temples in the city in his sixth consulship (Res Gestae 20.4), and that he built the temple of Mars Ultor and the Augustan Forum on his own land (21.1).
That last source is Augustus speaking about himself, so it tells us what he wanted remembered, not an independent assessment.
Read together, the passages show a ruler who presented rebuilding the city as part of rebuilding the state, which may be the point Dio was reaching for.

questions.q: How does Suetonius report the boast?
options: In indirect speech: not necessarily Augustus's exact words; he does not quote him directly
As a quotation from an inscription
He does not mention a boast

questions.q: What does Cassius Dio say Augustus meant by the remark?
options: The strength of the empire, not the buildings
Only the temples he had restored
The marble quarries he had opened

questions.q: In the Res Gestae, how many temples does Augustus say he rebuilt in his sixth consulship?
